children.translated_text: How is knowledge attained?
How will liberation come about?
And how is dispassion (<s>vairāgya</s>) obtained?
Tell me this, O Lord.
If you wish for liberation, dear one,
abandon sense-objects as poison,
forgiveness, straightforwardness, compassion, contentment,
and truth — embrace these as nectar.
You are neither earth, nor water, nor fire,

children.text: na vāyur dyaur na vā bhavān
children.translated_text: nor wind, nor sky — nor are you [any of] these.
Know the Self as the witness of these,
of the nature of consciousness, for the sake of liberation.

children.text: na vāyur dyaur na vā bhavān

children.translated_text: If, separating yourself from the body,
you rest in consciousness,
right now you will become happy, peaceful,
and free from bondage.
You are not a <s>brāhmaṇa</s> or any other <s>varṇa</s> (caste),
you are not in any <s>āśrama</s> (stage of life), nor an object of the senses.
You are unattached, formless —
the witness of the universe. Be happy!
<s>Dharma</s> (righteousness) and <s>adharma</s> (unrighteousness), pleasure and pain,
are of the mind, not yours, O all-pervading one.
You are neither the doer nor the enjoyer —
you are ever liberated.
You are the one seer of all,
and are virtually free at all times.
This alone is your bondage:
that you see another as the seer.
Bitten by the great black serpent
of the ego-sense "I am the doer,"
drink the antidote of the conviction
"I am not the doer," and be happy.
"I am the one pure awareness" —
with the fire of this certainty,
burn down the forest of ignorance.
Free from sorrow, be happy!
That in which this universe appears,
imagined like a snake in a rope —
that is bliss, supreme bliss.
That awareness is you — live happily!
One who considers oneself free is free indeed;
one who considers oneself bound is bound.
The saying here is true:
"As one's conviction, so one's destiny."
The Self is the witness, all-pervading, complete,
one, free, consciousness, actionless,
unattached, desireless, peaceful —
through delusion, it appears as if in <s>saṃsāra</s>.
Contemplate the Self as immutable (<s>kūṭastha</s>), awareness, non-dual,
and having abandoned the delusion
"I am a reflection,"
[abandon] both the external and the internal.
By the rope of identification with the body,
you have been long bound, dear child.
With the sword of the knowledge "I am awareness,"
cut that [bond] and be happy!
You are unattached, actionless,
self-luminous, stainless.
This alone is your bondage:
that you practice <s>samādhi</s> (meditation).
By you is this universe pervaded,
in you it is truly strung.
You are of the nature of pure, awakened essence —
do not resort to small-mindedness.
Without expectation, without modification,
firm, of cool disposition,
of unfathomable intelligence, undisturbed —
abide desiring consciousness alone.
Know that which has form to be unreal;
the formless alone is unchanging.
Through this instruction on truth,
there is no possibility of rebirth.
Just as a mirror exists both
within and around the reflection in it,
so too the Supreme Lord exists
within and around this body.
Just as the one all-pervading space
is both outside and inside a pot,
so the eternal, unbroken <s>Brahman</s>
is in all assemblages of beings.
Oh! I am stainless, peaceful,
awareness, beyond <s>prakṛti</s> (nature).
For all this time
I have been deceived by delusion alone!
Just as I, the one, illuminate
this body, so too [I illuminate] the world.
Therefore, the entire world is mine,
or else nothing whatsoever [is mine].
Oh! Having now abandoned the universe
together with the body,
by some skillful means alone
the Supreme Self is beheld.
Just as waves, foam, and bubbles
are not different from water,
so too the universe, arisen from the Self,
is not different from the Self.
A cloth, when examined,
is indeed nothing but thread;
so too this universe, when examined,
is nothing but the Self.
Just as sugar produced
in sugarcane juice is pervaded by it,
so too the universe, produced in me,
is pervaded by me without interruption.
From ignorance of the Self the world appears;
from knowledge of the Self it does not appear.
From ignorance of the rope a snake appears;
from knowledge of it, it does not appear.
Light is my own nature;
I am nothing other than that.
When the universe shines,
it is I alone who shine.
Oh! The universe appears in me
through ignorance, imagined —
like silver in a shell, a snake in a rope,
and water in a sunbeam.
The universe has emerged from me
and will dissolve back into me —
as a pot into clay, a wave into water,
and a bracelet into gold.
Oh, I bow to myself!
I who have no destruction,
who endures even when the entire world
from <s>Brahmā</s> to a blade of grass perishes.
Oh, I bow to myself!
I who am one, though embodied,
who neither goes nor comes anywhere,
yet abides pervading the universe.
Oh, I bow to myself!
There is none as skillful as I,
who sustains the universe forever
without touching it with the body.
Oh, I bow to myself!
I who possess nothing,
or I who possess everything
that is within the range of speech and mind.
Knowledge, the knowable, and the knower —
this triad does not truly exist.
That in which this [triad] appears through ignorance —
that stainless one am I.
Oh, suffering is rooted in duality!
There is no other remedy for it.
All this visible [world] is unreal —
I am the one, the essence of consciousness, immaculate.
I am awareness alone; through ignorance
a limiting adjunct (<s>upādhi</s>) has been imagined by me.
Reflecting thus constantly,
my abiding is in the thought-free [state].
For me there is neither bondage nor liberation;
the delusion has ceased, without support.
Oh, the universe rests in me,
yet in truth it does not rest in me.
This universe together with the body
is nothing — this is ascertained.
The Self is pure consciousness alone —
then what is there to imagine now?
The body, heaven and hell,
bondage and liberation, and also fear —
all this is mere imagination.
What concern is it to me, whose nature is consciousness?
Oh, even in a multitude of people,
I see no duality.
It has become like a wilderness —
where shall I direct my delight?
I am not the body, nor is the body mine.
I am not a <s>jīva</s> (individual soul) — I am consciousness.
This alone was my bondage:
the craving for life.
Oh, in me, the infinite great ocean,
when the wind of the mind rises,
the manifold waves of the world
suddenly arise.
In me, the infinite great ocean,
when the wind of the mind subsides,
the ship of the world, of the ill-fated merchant
that is the <s>jīva</s>, is destroyed.
In me, the infinite great ocean,
how wonderful — the waves that are <s>jīvas</s>
arise, collide, play,
and merge back, by their own nature.
Having known the Self as indestructible,
one, in truth —
how can you, a knower of the Self, a steadfast one,
take delight in the acquisition of wealth?
Oh, from ignorance of the Self
there is attachment to the realm of sense-object delusion,
just as from ignorance of the shell
there is greed for the illusory silver.
That in which this universe flashes forth
like waves in the ocean —
knowing "I am That,"
why do you run about like a wretched one?
Even after hearing that the Self
is pure consciousness, supremely beautiful,
one who remains attached to sensuality
attains impurity.
For the sage who knows the Self in all beings
and all beings in the Self —
it is astonishing
that the sense of "mine" persists.
Established in supreme non-duality,
even intent on liberation —
it is astonishing that, subject to desire,
one is enfeebled by the practice of amorous play.
Having recognized the enemy of knowledge
that has arisen, one who is exceedingly weak,
astonishingly, desires pleasure
even when approaching death.
For one who is dispassionate toward this world and the next,
who discriminates between the eternal and the non-eternal —
it is astonishing that one desiring liberation
is yet frightened of liberation itself.
But the steadfast one, whether being enjoyed
or being afflicted, at all times,
seeing only the Self alone,
is neither pleased nor angered.
The great-souled one sees his own body
acting as if it were another's body.
In praise as well as in blame,
how would such a one be agitated?
Seeing this universe as mere <s>māyā</s> (illusion),
devoid of curiosity,
even with death close at hand,
how would the one of steadfast wisdom be frightened?
For that great soul whose mind
is free from craving, even in despair —
who is satisfied by the knowledge of the Self —
with whom can he be compared?
Knowing by his very nature
that this visible [world] is nothing,
"this is to be grasped, this is to be rejected" —
what does the one of steadfast wisdom see?
For one who has internally abandoned all passions,
who is free from the pairs of opposites, free from desires —
enjoyment that comes spontaneously
is neither for suffering nor for satisfaction.
Indeed, for the Self-knower, the steadfast one,
who plays in the sport of enjoyment —
there is no equality whatsoever
with the deluded ones carried along by <s>saṃsāra</s>.
That state which the wretched ones —
<s>Indra</s> (<s>Śakra</s>) and all the gods — yearn to attain,
oh, the <s>yogin</s> established there
does not feel elation.
For the knower of That, neither merit nor sin
touches the inner [self],
just as smoke, though seen,
has no contact with the sky.
That great soul who has known
that this entire world is the Self alone —
who is capable of restraining him
as he lives spontaneously?
Among the fourfold group of beings
from <s>Brahmā</s> down to a blade of grass,
only the wise one indeed has the capacity
to renounce desire and aversion.
Rare is the one who knows
the non-dual Self as the Lord of the universe.
Such a one does whatever he knows [to be right],
and has no fear anywhere.
You have no attachment to anything;
being pure, what do you wish to renounce?
Dissolving the aggregate [of body and mind],
thus indeed enter dissolution.
From you the universe arises
like a bubble from the ocean.
Having thus known the one Self,
thus indeed enter dissolution.
Though perceived, the universe, being unreal,
does not exist in you who are pure.
Like a snake in a rope, clearly,
thus indeed enter dissolution.
Equal in suffering and happiness, fulfilled,
equal in hope and hopelessness,
equal in life and death —
thus indeed enter dissolution.
I am infinite like space;
the created world is like a pot.
Such is this knowledge — and of this [world],
there is neither rejection, nor grasping, nor dissolution.
I am like the great ocean;
the phenomenal world resembles waves.
Such is this knowledge — and of this [world],
there is neither rejection, nor grasping, nor dissolution.
I am like the mother-of-pearl;
the projection of the universe is like [illusory] silver.
Such is this knowledge — and of this [world],
there is neither rejection, nor grasping, nor dissolution.
I am in all beings,
and all beings are in me.
Such is this knowledge — and of this [world],
there is neither rejection, nor grasping, nor dissolution.
In me, the infinite great ocean,
the ship of the universe drifts here and there
driven by the wind of its own nature —
I have no impatience.
In me, the infinite great ocean,
the wave of the world, by its own nature,
let it rise or let it subside —

children.text: na me vṛddhir na ca kṣatiḥ
children.translated_text: I have neither increase nor loss.

children.text: na me vṛddhir na ca kṣatiḥ

children.translated_text: In me, the infinite great ocean,
the universe is but an imagining.
Supremely peaceful, formless —
in this alone I abide.
The Self is not in objects, nor are objects
in that infinite, stainless [Self].
Thus, unattached, desireless, peaceful —
in this alone I abide.
Oh, I am consciousness alone!
The world is like a magic show.
Therefore, how and where for me
could there be any imagining of rejection or acceptance?
Then there is bondage when the mind
desires something, grieves over something,
releases something, grasps something,
is delighted by something, or is angered by something.
Then there is liberation when the mind
does not desire, does not grieve,
does not release, does not grasp,
is not delighted, and is not angered.
Then there is bondage when the mind
is attached to any viewpoint.
Then there is liberation when the mind
is unattached to all viewpoints.
When there is no "I," there is liberation;
when there is "I," there is bondage.
Knowing this, with ease,
neither grasp nor release anything.
The dualities of done and undone —
when are they at peace, and for whom?
Having thus known, through disenchantment here,
become devoted to renunciation, free from vows.
Of some blessed soul, dear one,
through observing the activities of the world,
the desire for life, the hunger [for experience],
and the desire to know have subsided.
All this is indeed impermanent,
afflicted by the threefold suffering,
without essence, condemned, to be abandoned —
having ascertained this, one finds peace.
What is that time, what is that age
in which there are no dualities for human beings?
Disregarding them, one who lives
according to what comes would attain perfection.
The various opinions of the great sages,
saints, and <s>yogins</s> —
having seen [their diversity] and having attained disenchantment,
what person does not find peace?
Having accomplished the knowledge of the true form
of consciousness — is not [such a one] a <s>guru</s>?
One who, by the means of disenchantment, equanimity, and reason,
delivers from <s>saṃsāra</s> (worldly existence).
Behold the modifications of the elements —
they are nothing but the elements, in truth.
At that very instant, freed from bondage,
you will be established in your own nature.
Latent impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>) alone are <s>saṃsāra</s> —
therefore, release all of them.
That renunciation is [truly] through the renunciation of <s>vāsanās</s> (latent impressions);
abide now as you are.
Having abandoned desire, which is the enemy,
and wealth, which is fraught with misfortune,
and even <s>dharma</s>, which is the cause of these two —
practice indifference toward everything.
See as a dream or a magic show
three days or five —
friends, lands, wealth, homes,
wives, gifts, and other fortunes.
Wherever there is craving,
know that to be <s>saṃsāra</s> (worldly existence) indeed;
taking refuge in firm dispassion,
be free from craving and happy.
Bondage is nothing but craving;
its destruction is called <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation).
Through mere non-attachment to existence,
contentment with what is attained arises again and again.
You are the one, conscious, pure;
the universe is inert and unreal.
<s>Avidyā</s> (ignorance) too is nothing —
what desire to know, then, remains for you?
Kingdoms, sons, wives,
bodies, and pleasures —
though you were attached, these have perished
for you in birth after birth.
Enough with wealth, with desire,
and even with meritorious action!
In the wilderness of <s>saṃsāra</s>, through these,
the mind has found no rest.
In how many births has action been performed
by body, mind, and speech —
painful, toil-producing action?
Let it cease now, today!
Modification into existence and non-existence
is by nature — thus the one of firm conviction,
free from modification, free from affliction,
attains peace with ease.
'<s>Īśvara</s> (the Lord) is the creator of all;
there is no other here' — one of such firm conviction,
whose every desire has melted away within,
is at peace and clings to nothing anywhere.
'Misfortunes and fortunes come in their time
by fate alone' — one of such firm conviction,
content, with senses at rest, always
neither desires nor grieves.
'Pleasure and pain, birth and death
are by fate alone' — one of such firm conviction,
seeing nothing to be accomplished, free from toil,
even while acting, is not tainted.
'Suffering arises from worry;
from nothing else in this world' — one of such firm conviction,
free from that, is happy, peaceful,
with desire vanished everywhere.
'I am not the body, nor is the body mine;
I am awareness' — one of such firm conviction
has attained, as it were, <s>kaivalya</s> (absolute aloneness),
and does not remember what was done or not done.
'From <s>Brahmā</s> down to a blade of grass,
I alone am' — one of such firm conviction,
free from conceptualization, pure, peaceful,
is content with what is attained and what is not.
'This manifold universe is a wonder,
yet it is nothing' — one of such firm conviction,
free from <s>vāsanās</s> (latent impressions), mere spontaneous awareness,
is at peace, as if nothing at all.
First, unable to bear the actions of the body;
then, unable to bear the elaboration of speech;
then, unable to bear thought — thus
am I established, even so.
Through the absence of delight in sound and the rest,
and through the invisibility of the Self —
O one whose heart is [free from both] distraction and one-pointed concentration,
thus am I established, even so.
Distracted by <s>samādhi</s> (meditative absorption) and the like,
worldly activity for the sake of <s>samādhi</s> —
seeing this as merely a rule imposed,
thus am I established, even so.
Through the absence of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted,
and thus the absence of joy and sorrow —
O <s>Brahman</s>, today
thus am I established, even so.
<s>Āśrama</s> (stage of life) or non-<s>āśrama</s>, meditation,
the acceptance or rejection by the mind —
seeing these as my own conceptual constructions,
thus am I established, even so.
The performance of action is from ignorance,
just as its cessation is likewise;
having rightly understood this truth,
thus am I established, even so.
Even while thinking about the unthinkable,
one merely assumes the form of thought;
therefore, abandoning that meditation,
thus am I established, even so.
Whoever has acted even so,
that one becomes fulfilled.
Whoever has such a nature,
that one becomes fulfilled.
The well-being of possessing nothing
is rare even for one wearing only a loincloth.
Therefore, abandoning both renunciation and acquisition,
I abide as I please.
Sometimes the body is weary;
sometimes the tongue is weary;
sometimes the mind — abandoning all that,
I am established happily in the supreme goal.
'Nothing whatsoever has [really] been done' —
reflecting thus on the truth,
whatever comes to be done,
having done it, I abide as I please.
Embodied yogis are bound to insistence on
action or inaction;
free from both association and dissociation,
I abide as I please.
Neither benefit nor harm comes to me from standing,
walking, or lying down;
therefore, whether standing, walking, or sleeping,
I abide as I please.
There is no loss for me in sleeping,
nor accomplishment in striving;
therefore, abandoning [thoughts of] ruin and elation,
I abide as I please.
Having repeatedly observed the definite nature
of pleasure and the like in worldly conditions,
abandoning the auspicious and inauspicious,
I abide as I please.
One who is naturally empty-minded,
yet through inadvertence contemplates worldly existence,
is like one asleep who has been awakened —
for that one's recollection has been exhausted.
Where are riches? Where are friends?
Where are the sense-object thieves for me?
Where is scripture? Where is knowledge?
When all desire has dropped away from me.
Having known the witness <s>Puruṣa</s> (Self),
the <s>Paramātmā</s> (Supreme Self), the <s>Īśvara</s> (Lord),
and having become indifferent to bondage and liberation,
there is no concern for my liberation.
One who is void of conceptualization within
yet wanders freely without —
the various states of such a one, appearing as if deluded,
only those of like nature can understand.
An intelligent being of good disposition is fulfilled
by instruction given in any manner whatsoever;
but another, inquiring throughout a lifetime,
remains bewildered therein.
<s>Mokṣa</s> (liberation) is dispassion toward sense-objects;
bondage is relishing of sense-objects.
This alone is knowledge —
now do as you wish.
This realization of truth renders
the eloquent, learned, and industrious person
mute, dull, and idle;
therefore it is shunned by those who desire enjoyment.

children.text: na tvaṃ deho na te deho
children.translated_text: You are not the body, nor is the body yours;
you are neither the enjoyer nor the doer.
You are consciousness itself, the eternal witness,
without need — wander happily.

children.text: na tvaṃ deho na te deho

children.translated_text: Attachment and aversion are properties of the mind;
the mind is never yours.
You are free from conceptualization, the Self of awareness,
changeless — wander happily.
Knowing the Self in all beings
and all beings in the Self,
free from ego-sense,
free from 'mine' — be happy.
That in which this universe appears
like waves in the ocean —
that is you yourself, there is no doubt.
O one whose form is consciousness, be free from fever!
Have faith, dear one, have faith!
Do not be deluded in this, O good one!
You are the Lord, whose very nature is knowledge,
the Self, beyond <s>Prakṛti</s> (primordial nature).
The body, enveloped by the <s>guṇas</s> (qualities),
stays, comes, and goes;
the Self neither goes nor comes —
why do you grieve for it?
Let the body remain until the end of the <s>kalpa</s> (eon),
or let it depart even today —

children.text: kva vṛddhiḥ kva ca vā hānis
children.translated_text: where is increase, where is decrease
for you, whose form is pure consciousness?

children.text: kva vṛddhiḥ kva ca vā hānis

children.translated_text: In you, the infinite great ocean,
the wave of the universe naturally
rises and subsides —

children.text: na te vṛddhir na vā kṣatiḥ
children.translated_text: there is neither increase nor loss for you.

children.text: na te vṛddhir na vā kṣatiḥ

children.translated_text: Dear one, you are of the form of pure consciousness;
this world is not separate from you.
Therefore, for whom, how, and where
is the imagining of what is to be rejected and accepted?
In the one, imperishable, peaceful,
stainless space of consciousness that is you —
whence is birth, whence is action,
and whence even the ego?
Whatever you see, in that
you alone are reflected.
Does a bracelet, armlet, or anklet
shine apart from gold?
'This I am, this I am not' —
abandon such discrimination.
Having ascertained that all is the Self,
be free from conceptual construction and happy.
The universe exists only through your ignorance;
in reality, you alone are.
There is no other who transmigrates,
nor one who does not transmigrate.
This universe is mere delusion,
it is nothing — one of such firm conviction,
free from <s>vāsanās</s> (latent impressions), mere spontaneous awareness,
is at peace, as if nothing at all.
One alone in the ocean of existence
was, is, and will be.
There is neither bondage nor liberation for you —
fulfilled, wander happily.
Do not agitate the mind
with acceptance and rejection, O one made of consciousness!
Be calm, abide happily
in the Self, the embodiment of bliss.
Abandon meditation altogether;
hold nothing in the heart.
You are the Self, ever liberated —
what will you accomplish by deliberating?
Recite or listen, dear one,
to the various scriptures many times over;
yet there is no peace for you
apart from the forgetting of everything.
Pursue enjoyment, action, or <s>samādhi</s> (meditative absorption),
O wise one — yet still
the mind, freed from all desires,
will yearn exceedingly [for peace].
Everyone is unhappy from exertion —
no one knows this.
By this very teaching alone
the blessed one attains contentment.
One who finds even the blinking
and opening of the eyes wearisome —
for that champion of laziness alone
there is happiness, for no one else.
'This has been done, this has not' —
when the mind is freed from such dualities,
toward <s>dharma</s>, wealth, desire, and <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation)
it becomes indifferent.
The dispassionate one is an enemy of sense-objects;
the passionate one is greedy for sense-objects.
But one who is free from both grasping and releasing
is neither dispassionate nor passionate.
The notion of what is to be rejected and accepted
is the sprout of the tree of <s>saṃsāra</s>.
Desire lives as long as
one's state is the ground of non-inquiry.
In activity, attachment arises;
in cessation, aversion indeed.
The wise one, free from dualities, like a child,
is established even so.
The passionate one wishes to abandon <s>saṃsāra</s>
out of desire to escape suffering;
but the dispassionate one, being free from suffering,
does not feel distressed even in it.
One who has pride even regarding <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation),
and possessiveness regarding the body —

children.text: na ca jñānī na vā yogī
children.translated_text: is neither a knower nor a yogin,
but merely a partaker of suffering.

children.text: na ca jñānī na vā yogī

children.translated_text: Even if <s>Hara</s> (<s>Śiva</s>) were your teacher,
or <s>Hari</s> (<s>Viṣṇu</s>), or the lotus-born (<s>Brahmā</s>),
yet there is no peace for you
apart from the forgetting of everything.
That one has attained the fruit of knowledge
and likewise the fruit of yoga practice,
who is content, with pure senses, always
delighting alone in solitude.
Never in this world does the knower of truth
suffer, alas;
for by that one alone is this
entire sphere of the universe filled.
Sense-objects never gladden
one who delights in the Self —
just as <s>nimba</s> (neem) leaves [do not please]
an elephant delighted by <s>sallakī</s> (Indian frankincense) leaves.
One who, having enjoyed enjoyments,
is not habituated to them,
and who is free from longing for what is unenjoyed —
such a one is rare in the world.
In this world, those who desire enjoyment
and those who desire liberation are both seen;
but one who desires neither enjoyment nor liberation,
such a great-minded one is rare indeed.
Toward <s>dharma</s>, wealth, desire, <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation),
as toward life and death —
for one of noble mind
there is no notion of what is to be rejected or accepted.
There is no wish for the dissolution of the universe,
nor aversion to its continuance;
therefore, living as it comes, the blessed one
abides happily, as one pleases.
'I am fulfilled by this knowledge' —
thus the accomplished one, whose intellect has dissolved,
seeing, hearing, touching, smelling,
and eating, abides as one pleases.
Empty gaze, purposeless activity,
and enfeebled senses —
neither craving nor dispassion
for one whose ocean of <s>saṃsāra</s> has dried up.
Neither waking nor sleeping,
neither opening the eyes nor closing them —
ah, a transcendent state exists somewhere
for one whose mind is liberated.
Everywhere appearing self-composed,
everywhere with pure intention,
freed from all <s>vāsanās</s> (latent impressions),
the liberated one shines everywhere.
Seeing, hearing, touching, smelling,
eating, taking, speaking, walking —
freed from the desired and undesired,
the great-minded one is liberated indeed.
Neither blaming nor praising,
neither rejoicing nor being angered,
neither giving nor taking —
the liberated one is dispassionate everywhere.
Seeing an amorous woman
or death approaching —
unperturbed in mind, self-composed,
the great-minded one is liberated indeed.
In pleasure or pain, in man or woman,
in prosperity or adversity —
there is no distinction for the steadfast one
who sees equally everywhere.
Neither harm nor compassion,
neither arrogance nor humility,
neither wonder nor agitation
in one whose wandering in <s>saṃsāra</s> has been exhausted.
The liberated one is not an enemy of sense-objects,
nor greedy for sense-objects;
with mind ever unattached,
one enjoys what comes and what does not.
Conceptualizations of <s>samādhi</s> (concentration) and non-<s>samādhi</s>,
of beneficial and harmful —
the empty-minded one does not know these,
established, as it were, in <s>kaivalya</s> (absolute aloneness).
Free from 'mine,' free from ego,
convinced that nothing exists,
all desires melted away within —
even while acting, one does not act.
Free from the illumination, delusion,
sleep, and dullness of the mind —
having attained a state beyond description,
one whose mind has dissolved.
For one upon whose awakening
delusion becomes as if a dream —
to that one whose sole form is bliss,
homage to that peaceful radiance!
Even after acquiring all objects
one obtains abundant enjoyments —
yet one cannot become happy
without the complete renunciation of all.
For one whose inner self is scorched
by the blazing sun of the pain of duty,
whence is happiness without the shower
of the nectar-rain of tranquility?
This existence is mere imagination;
it is nothing in the ultimate sense.
There is no non-existence for those whose nature is existence.
of those who perceive existence and non-existence.
Not far away, nor through contraction,
the state of the Self is already attained —
free from conceptualization, free from effort,
changeless, untainted.
Merely by the cessation of delusion,
merely by the recognition of one's own nature,
they shine forth, free from sorrow,
with unveiled vision.
All of this is mere imagination;
the <s>Ātman</s> (Self) is liberated, eternal.
Knowing this, the wise one —
why would he practice like a child?
Having ascertained that the <s>Ātman</s> is <s>Brahman</s>,
and that existence and non-existence are imagined,
one who is desireless — what does he know?
What does he say? What does he do?
'This I am,' 'This I am not' —
such conceptual distinctions are extinguished.
Having ascertained that all is the Self,
for the <s>yogin</s> who has become silent —
there is neither distraction nor one-pointedness,
neither super-knowledge nor stupidity,

children.text: na sukhaṃ na ca vā duḥkham
children.translated_text: neither pleasure nor pain,
for the <s>yogin</s> who is at peace.

children.text: na sukhaṃ na ca vā duḥkham

children.translated_text: In sovereignty or in the life of a beggar,
in gain or loss, in society or in the forest,
for the <s>yogin</s> whose nature is free from conceptualization,
there is no distinction.

children.text: kva dharmaḥ kva ca vā kāmaḥ
children.translated_text: Where is <s>dharma</s> (duty)? Where indeed is <s>kāma</s> (desire)?
Where is <s>artha</s> (wealth)? Where is discrimination?
'This has been done,' 'This has not' —
for the <s>yogin</s> who is free from all pairs of opposites.

children.text: kva dharmaḥ kva ca vā kāmaḥ

children.translated_text: There is nothing whatsoever to be done,
nor any attachment in the heart.
Living just as life comes,
such is the <s>yogin</s> who is liberated while living (<s>jīvanmukta</s>).

children.text: kva mohaḥ kva ca vā viśvaṃ
children.translated_text: Where is delusion? Where indeed is the world?
Where is meditation? Where is liberation?
For the great soul (<s>mahātman</s>) who has come to rest
at the boundary of all intentions —

children.text: kva mohaḥ kva ca vā viśvaṃ

children.translated_text: he by whom this world was seen,
let him declare 'it does not exist.'
One who is free from impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>) — what does he do?
Even seeing, he does not see.
He who has seen the Supreme <s>Brahman</s> —
should he think 'I am <s>Brahman</s>'?
What does the thought-free one think,
who does not see a second?
He by whom the distraction of the Self is seen
undertakes its cessation.
But the noble one, not being distracted —
in the absence of anything to accomplish, what does he do?
The wise one, though contrary to the world,
even while acting in worldly ways,
sees neither <s>samādhi</s> (absorption) nor distraction
nor any taint in himself.
The wise one (<s>budha</s>) who is devoid of
existence and non-existence, content, free from impressions —
nothing is done by him,
even though he appears to act in the eyes of the world.
In engagement or withdrawal,
the wise one indeed has no stubbornness.
Whatever comes to be done,
having done it, he abides in happiness.
Free from impressions, without support,
self-willed, freed from bondage,
tossed by the wind of latent impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>),
he moves like a dry leaf.
For one who is beyond <s>saṃsāra</s> (worldly existence), nowhere
is there joy or sorrow.
With a mind always cool,
he shines as if bodiless (<s>videha</s>).
Nowhere is there the wish to abandon,
nor is there destruction anywhere,
for the wise one who delights in the Self (<s>ātmārāma</s>),
whose nature is cool and transparent.
For the wise one whose mind is empty by nature,
acting spontaneously,
like an ordinary person,
there is neither pride nor humiliation.
'This action was done by the body,
not by me who am of pure nature' —
one who is devoted to such reflection,
even while acting, does not act.
He acts as if he were not speaking of that,
and yet he is not a fool.
Liberated while living (<s>jīvanmukta</s>), happy, prosperous,
he shines even while wandering in <s>saṃsāra</s>.
Wearied by various deliberations,
the wise one has come to rest.
He does not imagine, does not know,
does not hear, does not see.
Being neither in <s>samādhi</s> nor in distraction,
he is neither a seeker of liberation nor otherwise.
Having ascertained that all perceived is imagined,
the great-souled one abides as <s>Brahman</s> alone.
He who has ego (<s>ahaṅkāra</s>) within —
even not acting, he acts.
But for the wise one free from ego,
nothing is left undone even while doing nothing.
Neither agitated nor content,
non-doer, free from movement,
without hope, free from doubt —
the mind of the liberated one shines.
The mind does not engage
in meditation or in activity,
yet without cause, it nevertheless
meditates and acts.
Having heard the truth as it truly is,
the dull one attains only bewilderment,
or else attains a kind of withdrawal
that an un-deluded one [might mistake] for confusion.
One-pointedness and cessation
are practiced strenuously by the deluded.
The wise do not see anything to be done,
established in their own state, like one asleep.
Neither through effort nor through effortlessness
does the deluded one attain tranquility.
Merely through the ascertainment of truth,
the wise one becomes tranquil.
Pure, awakened, beloved, complete,
beyond elaboration, free from affliction —
people who are devoted to practice
do not know that Self.
The thoroughly deluded one does not attain liberation
through action in the form of practice.
The blessed one, through knowledge alone,
remains liberated and free from modification.
The deluded one does not attain that <s>Brahman</s>
which he desires to become.
The wise one, even without desiring,
partakes of the nature of the Supreme <s>Brahman</s>.
Without support, busy with grasping,
the deluded ones nourish <s>saṃsāra</s>.
The root of this root of all misfortune
has been cut by the wise.
The deluded one does not find peace
even when he strives for tranquility.
The wise one, having ascertained the truth,
is always of a peaceful mind.
Where is the vision of the Self for one
who clings to what is seen?
The wise do not see this or that;
they see only the imperishable Self.
Where is cessation for the deluded one
who persists in restraint?
For the wise one who delights in the Self,
it is always effortless and natural.
Some are meditators on existence,
others meditate on nothing.
Rare is the one who meditates on neither —
thus he is undisturbed.
Those of poor understanding meditate upon
the Self as pure and non-dual,
but they do not know it, due to delusion,
and remain unfulfilled throughout life.
The intellect of the seeker of liberation
cannot exist without a support.
But the intellect of the liberated one is always
without support and without desire.
Seeing the tigers of sense-objects,
those who are frightened and seek refuge
quickly enter the cave
for the attainment of cessation and one-pointedness.
Seeing the lion free from impressions,
the elephant-like sense-objects
flee silently, unable [to approach],
or serve him with flattery.
The one whose mind is composed, free from anxiety,
does not hold to practices for liberation.
Seeing, hearing, touching, smelling,
eating — he abides at ease.
Merely by hearing the reality of things,
one of pure intellect becomes undisturbed.
He sees neither proper conduct, nor misconduct,
nor indifference.
Whatever comes to be done,
the straightforward one does that.
Whether auspicious or inauspicious,
his actions are like those of a child.
Through freedom (<s>svātantrya</s>), one attains happiness;
through freedom, one attains the supreme;
through freedom, one reaches tranquility;
through freedom, the highest state.
When one realizes the non-doership
and non-enjoyership of one's own Self,
then indeed all modifications
of the mind come to an end.
The unrestrained, artless
abiding of the wise one shines.
Not so the artificial peace
of the deluded one whose mind is full of longing.
They revel in great enjoyments,
they enter mountain caves —
the wise, free from conceptualization,
unbound, with liberated minds.
Upon seeing a learned <s>brāhmaṇa</s>, a deity, a sacred place,
a woman, a king, a beloved —
the wise one, having paid respect,
harbors no impression (<s>vāsanā</s>) in his heart.
Though ridiculed and scorned by servants,
sons, wives, grandchildren, and kinsmen,
the <s>yogin</s>
is not in the least disturbed.
Though content, he is not content;
though afflicted, he is not afflicted.
That wondrous state of his
is known only by those of like nature.
The sense of 'something to be done' is <s>saṃsāra</s> itself;
the wise do not see it.
Empty in form, formless,
changeless, free from affliction.
Though doing nothing, the dull-witted one
is agitated and distracted everywhere.
But even while performing actions,
the skillful one is indeed undisturbed.
He sits happily, sleeps happily,
happily comes and goes,
happily speaks, happily eats —
even in worldly dealings, his mind is at peace.
One who by nature has no suffering
even while engaging in worldly affairs —
like a great lake, unshakable,
free from afflictions, he shines beautifully.
Even the withdrawal of the deluded one
gives rise to engagement.
Even the engagement of the wise one
bears the fruit of withdrawal.
Dispassion toward possessions
is mostly seen in the deluded.
For one whose hope regarding the body has vanished,
where is attachment? Where is dispassion?
The vision of the deluded is always
attached to meditation and non-meditation.
But that [vision], by virtue of what is to be contemplated,
is in the form of non-seeing for one who is self-abiding.
The sage who moves about without desire
in all undertakings, like a child —
no taint clings to that pure one,
even in the midst of performing action.
He alone is blessed, the knower of the Self,
who is equal toward all states of being.
Seeing, hearing, touching, smelling,
eating — his mind is free from craving.
Where is <s>saṃsāra</s>? Where is appearance?
Where is the goal? Where is the means?
For the wise one who is like space,
always free from conceptualization.
Victorious is the one who has renounced objects of pursuit,
whose embodiment is the fullness of one's own essence (<s>svarasa</s>).
Unaffected, in uninterrupted
<s>samādhi</s> (absorption) he abides.
What more need be said here?
The great-souled one who has known the truth
is free from longing for both enjoyment and liberation,
always indifferent everywhere.
The duality of the world, beginning with <s>mahat</s> (the great principle),
is but an expansion of mere names.
Having abandoned [all that], for one of pure awakening,
what duty remains?
All this is the product of delusion;
nothing exists — such is his firm conviction.
With imperceptible radiance, pure,
he naturally becomes tranquil.
For one whose form is pure radiance,
who does not see the existence of the visible —
where is injunction? Where is dispassion?
Where is renunciation? Where indeed is tranquility?
For one who shines forth in infinite form
and does not see material nature (<s>prakṛti</s>) —

children.text: kva bandhaḥ kva ca vā mokṣaḥ
children.translated_text: where is bondage? Where is liberation?
Where is joy? Where is sorrow?

children.text: kva bandhaḥ kva ca vā mokṣaḥ

children.translated_text: In <s>saṃsāra</s>, which extends only as far as the intellect,
only <s>māyā</s> (illusion) appears as transformation.
Without 'mine,' without ego,
desireless, the wise one shines.
For the sage who sees the Self
as imperishable and free from sorrow —

children.text: kva vidyā ca kva vā viśvaṃ
children.translated_text: where is knowledge? Where is the world?
Where is the body, or 'I' and 'mine'?

children.text: kva vidyā ca kva vā viśvaṃ

children.translated_text: If the dull-witted one abandons
actions such as cessation and the like,
he falls into daydreams and prattle
from that very moment.
The dull one, even upon hearing that truth,
does not abandon his delusion.
Outwardly thought-free by effort,
he craves for objects within.
One whose actions have fallen away through knowledge,
even though performing actions in the world's eyes,
finds no occasion to do
or even to say anything.
Where is darkness? Where is light?
Where is abandonment? Nothing whatsoever [exists]
for the wise one who is changeless,
always free from anxiety.
Where is fortitude? Where is discrimination?
Where indeed is even fearlessness?
For the <s>yogin</s> whose nature is inexpressible,
who is without [any fixed] nature.
There is no heaven, there is no hell,
nor indeed is there liberation while living.
What more need be said here?
From the perspective of <s>yoga</s>, nothing [exists] at all.
He neither desires gain
nor grieves at loss.
The mind of the wise one is cool,
as if filled with nectar (<s>amṛta</s>).
The desireless one neither praises the peaceful
nor blames the wicked.
Equal in pleasure and pain, content,
he sees nothing to be done.
The wise one neither hates <s>saṃsāra</s>
nor wishes to see the Self.
Free from elation and anger,
he is neither dead nor alive.
Without affection for children and wife,
without desire for sense objects,
without care even for his own body,
without expectation — the wise one shines.
Contentment is everywhere for the wise one
who lives as circumstances bring.
Wandering freely through lands,
sleeping wherever the sun sets.
Let the body fall or rise —
the great soul has no concern for it,
resting in the ground of his own nature,
having forgotten all worldly existence.
Possessing nothing, moving at will,
free from dualities, with doubts cut asunder,
unattached to all states of being,
the wise one rejoices in solitude.
Without 'mine,' the wise one shines,
equal toward a clod of earth, a stone, and gold.
The knot of the heart well cut,
<s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s> thoroughly shaken off.
For one who is everywhere inattentive [to worldly things],
there is no impression (<s>vāsanā</s>) whatsoever in the heart.
Who can compare to the liberated soul
who is fully satisfied?
Though knowing, he does not know;
though seeing, he does not see;
though speaking, he does not speak —
who else [is there] other than one free from impressions?
Whether a mendicant or a king,
one who is desireless, he shines.
For one in whom the notions of good and bad
regarding things have dropped away —
where is freedom? Where is restraint?
Where is the determination of truth?
For the <s>yogin</s> who is guileless, straightforward, and natural,
whose purpose is fulfilled.
By one who is content in the repose of the Self,
without expectation, free from suffering —
what is experienced within,
how and to whom can it be told?
Even in sleep, he is not in deep sleep;
even in sleep, he does not sleep;
even in waking, he does not wake —
the wise one is content at every step.
The knower, though with thought, is free from thought;
though with senses, is without senses;
though with intellect, is without intellect;
though with ego, is free from ego-sense.

children.text: na sukhī na ca vā duḥkhī
children.translated_text: Neither happy nor unhappy,
neither detached nor attached,
neither a seeker of liberation nor liberated —
he is nothing and yet everything.

children.text: na sukhī na ca vā duḥkhī

children.translated_text: Even in distraction, he is not distracted;
even in <s>samādhi</s> (meditative absorption), he is not in <s>samādhi</s>;
even in dullness, the blessed one is not dull;
even in learning, he is not a scholar.
The liberated one, established in his natural state,
fulfilled in having done what is to be done,
equal everywhere through desirelessness,
does not remember what was done or not done.
He is not pleased when praised,
nor angered when blamed;
he is not alarmed at death,
nor does he rejoice in life.
He does not rush toward crowds of people,
nor toward the forest — his mind at peace;
however and wherever [he may be],
he remains the same.
With the tongs of the knowledge of reality (<s>tattvavijñāna</s>),
from the cavity of the heart,
the thorn of manifold anxious thoughts
has been extracted by me.

children.text: kva dharmaḥ kva ca vā kāmaḥ
children.translated_text: Where is <s>dharma</s> (righteousness)? Where is desire (<s>kāma</s>)?
Where is wealth (<s>artha</s>)? Where is discrimination?
Where is duality? And where indeed is non-duality? —
for me who abide in my own glory.

children.text: kva dharmaḥ kva ca vā kāmaḥ

children.translated_text: Where is the past? Where the future?
Where indeed even the present?

children.text: kva deśaḥ kva ca vā nityaṃ
children.translated_text: Where is space? Where indeed is eternity? —
for me who abide in my own glory.

children.text: kva deśaḥ kva ca vā nityaṃ

children.translated_text: Where is the self? Where the non-self?
Where is the auspicious? Where the inauspicious?
Where is worry? Where non-worry? —
for me who abide in my own glory.
Where is dream? Where is deep sleep?
Where likewise is waking?
Where is the fourth state (<s>turīya</s>)? Or where is fear? —
for me who abide in my own glory.
Where is far? Where is near?
Where is outer? Where is inner?

children.text: kva sthūlaṃ kva ca vā sūkṣmaṃ
children.translated_text: Where is gross? Where is subtle? —
for me who abide in my own glory.

children.text: kva sthūlaṃ kva ca vā sūkṣmaṃ

children.translated_text: Where is death? Or where is life?
Where are worlds? Where is worldly [existence]?
Where is dissolution? Where is <s>samādhi</s>? —
for me who abide in my own glory.
Enough of talk about the three goals (<s>trivarga</s>);
enough of talk about <s>yoga</s>;
enough of talk about knowledge (<s>vijñāna</s>) —
for me who rest in the Self.
Where are the elements? Where the body?
Where the senses? Where the mind?
Where is the void? Where is despair? —
in my own nature, which is stainless.
Where is scripture (<s>śāstra</s>)? Where self-knowledge?
Where is the mind free from objects?
Where is contentment? Where desirelessness? —
for me who have forever transcended the pairs of opposites.
Where is knowledge (<s>vidyā</s>)? Where is ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>)?
Where is 'I'? Where is 'this'? Where is 'mine'?

children.text: kva bandhaḥ kva ca vā mokṣaḥ
children.translated_text: Where is bondage? Where is liberation?
Where is any form for the Self's own nature?

children.text: kva bandhaḥ kva ca vā mokṣaḥ

children.translated_text: Where are commenced <s>karmas</s> (<s>prārabdha</s>)?
Where indeed is <s>jīvanmukti</s> (liberation while living)?
Where is that bodiless isolation (<s>videhakaivalya</s>)? —
for one who is always without distinctions.

children.text: kva kartā kva ca vā bhoktā
children.translated_text: Where is the doer? Where the enjoyer?
Where is actionless shining forth?
Where is direct [realization]? Or where is its fruit? —
for me who am always without any inherent nature.

children.text: kva kartā kva ca vā bhoktā

children.translated_text: Where is the world? Where the seeker of liberation?
Where is the <s>yogin</s>? Where the knower?

children.text: kva baddhaḥ kva ca vā muktaḥ
children.translated_text: Where is the bound one? Where the liberated? —
I am non-dual in my own essential nature.

children.text: kva baddhaḥ kva ca vā muktaḥ

children.translated_text: Where is creation? Where is destruction?
Where is the goal? Where is the means?
Where is the seeker? Where is attainment? —
I am non-dual in my own essential nature.
Where is the knower? Where the means of knowledge?
Where is the object of knowledge? Where is cognition?

children.text: kva kiṃcit kva na kiṃcid vā
children.translated_text: Where is something? Where is nothing? —
for me who am always pure.

children.text: kva kiṃcit kva na kiṃcid vā

children.translated_text: Where is distraction? Where is one-pointedness?
Where is non-understanding? Where is delusion?
Where is joy? Where is sorrow? —
for me who am always without action.
Where indeed is this conventional [reality]?
Where is that ultimate reality?

children.text: kva sukhaṃ kva ca vā dukhaṃ
children.translated_text: Where is pleasure? Where is pain? —
for me who am always free from deliberation.

children.text: kva sukhaṃ kva ca vā dukhaṃ

children.translated_text: Where is <s>māyā</s> (illusion)? Where is <s>saṃsāra</s> (worldly existence)?
Where is attachment? Where is detachment?
Where is the <s>jīva</s> (individual soul)? Where is <s>Brahman</s>? —
for me who am always pure.
Where is activity? Or cessation?
Where is liberation? Where is bondage? —
for me who am unchanging (<s>kūṭastha</s>), without parts,
established in myself always.
Where is instruction? Where is scripture?

children.text: kva śiṣyaḥ kva ca vā guruḥ
children.translated_text: Where is the disciple? Where is the teacher?
Where indeed is the purpose of human life (<s>puruṣārtha</s>)? —
for me who am auspicious (<s>Śiva</s>), free from all limiting adjuncts.

children.text: kva śiṣyaḥ kva ca vā guruḥ
kva cāsti kva ca vā nāsti
children.translated_text: Where is existence? Where is non-existence?
Where is oneness? Where is duality?
What need to say more?
Nothing whatsoever arises for me.

children.text: kva cāsti kva ca vā nāsti
